newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union vows to bring Chrysler deal to Ford, GM.
newsitem.headline: Canada union vows to bring Chrysler deal to Ford, GM.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers union, fresh from a tentative deal with Chrysler Corp., now faces the tougher challenge of pressing its newly won contract terms on Ford Motor Co. and General Motors Corp..
Auto industry analysts said it will be tough for the union to sell the deal it negotiated with Chrysler Canada to the Canadian units of Ford and GM.
"It creates something, which is going to be hell for them to sell at Ford and GM," said Daniel Luria of Michigan's Industrial Technology Institute. "But it establishes the principle they want."
The CAW will disclose its next negotiating target on Monday and has said the strike deadline will be 10 days from the announcement.

Key to the union's settlement with Chrysler was the language on shifting work to outside companies, a practice known as outsourcing. The pact prevents Chrysler Canada from cutting any jobs or selling any plants during the life of the three-year agreement.
The 12,600 unionized Chrysler Canada workers vote on the deal on Sunday.
Contract language obtained by Reuters specifically sets out the restrictions on shifting work to outside suppliers:
"The Company commits there will be no reduction in employment levels as a result of outsourcing during the term of this agreement."

A side letter from Chrysler negotiator Ken Francese to CAW President Buzz Hargrove, stated, "As a result of your deep concern ... this will confirm that during the life of the new collective bargaining agreement, until Sept. 14, 1999, the company will not close or sell any plant, in whole or in part, covered by this collective agreement."

Luria said a plus for the CAW is that the outsourcing restrictions may be easier for the Canadian companies to swallow because their parent firms could use outside suppliers and shed jobs in the United States.
"It's going to be easier to sell, because in Canada Ford and GM don't make a lot of parts," Luria said.

GM Canada spokesman Greg Gibson said the automaker intends to proceed with plans to sell its Oshawa and Windsor, Ontario, parts plants as well as other moves that would affect a total of more than 5,000 jobs.
"At this point in time those plants are up for sale and we are talking with interested parties," Gibson said.
He said job security at GM Canada would need to be tied to the company's competitiveness. Hargrove vowed to apply to GM the language of the Chrysler agreement.
"Our history of bargaining in this industry is that once a pattern has been established, that becomes the pattern for the total industry," said Hargrove.

Gibson said, "I think we'll have to really sit down and talk about it. There are some difficult issues on the table and we have a lot of hard work in front of us both from our perspective and from the CAW's."
The CAW said its outsourcing proposal was less of a concern for Ford than GM because Ford has no known plans to shift work to outside suppliers in Canada.
"At Ford and Chrysler the outsourcing issue is one of setting the principle, but at General Motors we have the added problem of the practical," Hargrove said.

The CAW said the deal struck with Chrysler late Tuesday included a 2 percent wage increase in each year of a three-year contract and improved health care benefits, but did not yield to Chrysler's demands for user fees, co-payments and caps on the health and benefit plans.
Ford of Canada officials said they would not comment on their position without seeing the Chrsyler contract.
Ford's stock fell 25 cents to $32.125, while Chrysler was unchanged at $28.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
